newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council calls for preparation of Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council calls for preparation of Zaire force.

text.p: The Security Council early on Saturday called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help end the crisis in eastern Zaire but postponed its deployment until a later stage.
The interim resolution, adopted unanimously, asked the states involved to report back as soon as possible to enable the council to give final approval.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, was asked to draw up a "concept of operations and framework for a humanitarian task force" to get aid to more than one million refugees from ethnic violence in Rwanda and Burundi and to plan for their voluntary repatriation. He is to report to the council by a Nov. 20 deadline.

Many council members had hoped to adopt a resolution authorising the immediate creation of a multinational force to deal with a catastrophe of biblical proportions that has already claimed thousands of lives.

But this was impossible after the United States, mindful of its involvement in an ill-fated humanitarian operation in Somalia, said it was still studying whether it could participate and if so whether with logistics, financial assistance or other means.
Diplomats said U.S. airlift capability would be a vital contribution to the operation.

Stressing the need for careful preparation, U.S. envoy Karl Inderfurth told reporters after the vote: "We believe that a carefully planned and coordinated international force can make a critical contribution. This resolution lays the basis for such a force and we support it."

Stressing the need to resolve the underlying problems that sparked the crisis, he added: "We must seek a more lasting solution which not only provides for the delivery of humanitarian assistance but also provides for the secure and orderly repatriation of refugees."

Britain's ambassador, Sir John Weston, also said the aim was "both to address the question of immediate humanitarian aid to those who are literally dying on their feet and to help create the conditions for the orderly return of refugees to their countries of origin."
He said Britain wished to help but "exactly how we do that remains to be decided."

Boutros-Ghali, who has repeatedly called for swift action by the council, said the refugees, scattered by recent fighting in eastern Zaire, were without food, water or shelter and faced "genocide by starvation."

The council resolution was adopted shortly before 2 am EST (0700 GMT) at a meeting without speeches that lasted only a few minutes. But it was preceded by daylong consultations that stretched beyond midnight.

No figure was given for the size of the proposed force, whose command and financing would be up to the participating countries. All U.N. members would be encouraged to contribute to the operation in any way possible.
Diplomats have said between 4,000 and 5,000 troops would be needed to carry out the operation in the turbulent Central African region.

France and Spain have already said they could send 1,000 men each. However, Rwanda's Tutsi government is mistrustful of France as an ally of the Hutu government ousted after genocidal massacres in 1994.
Zaire has said it would no longer allow Rwandan and Burundian refugees to re-establish camps on its territory and that they must be repatriated.
A longer range objective spelled out in the resolution is the convening of an international conference to resolve the problems of the African Great Lakes region that spawned the current crisis.

Hundreds of thousands of people fled to eastern Zaire after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda two years ago while thousands more escaped continuing violence between Hutus and Tutsis in neighbouring Burundi.

The Rwandan refugees include still-armed members of the former Hutu-led army and militia responsible for the 1994 killings who fear retribution if they return home. They have used force to prevent other Hutus from being repatriated.
Thousands of other refugees have fled recent fighting between the Zairean army and Zairean ethnic Tutsis, backed by the Rwandan army.
